blocks.x: I'll make a note down here that we're recording an interview with Mr. Sylvester Handy at his home at 1825.
1825. Carnot, is that it? How do they pronounce that? Carnot. C-A-N-N-O-T. Carnot. C-A-R-N-O-T.
C-A-R-N-O-T. And this is Bill Russell speaking, and the date is December the 13th, 1961. Right. So can you give your full name, Mr. Hand, if you have a middle name?
Sylvester George Hand.

Do you mind telling just when you were born, in what city, if it was right here in town or where? Paschristian, Mississippi. Up in Paschristian, Mississippi. I knew that you'd spent some time over there, and that your brothers had too.
That's right, and I've been here since, since 27. 1927. How old are you now? I'm 58 now.
58. What is your birthday?
September the 8th.
September the 8th. Can you tell me anything about your family? Did your father play music? I know several of the brothers.
Well, the whole family was musical. The whole family. Mother, father, sister, brothers. All the whole family was musical. What was your father's name? What did he play? John Hand.
That's what I thought. John Hand Sr. was named after him. That's right.
What did he play? All instruments. Oh really? All instruments.
All instruments.
Violin, he was a professional violin player. Chin violin, not bass violin.
Yeah, the regular little violin.

Regular violin, uh-huh. And mandolin and guitar. He was, he was just a genius, but not with notes. He was an air man. Just played by air man. By air man. But that's the way we were right up. We were right up until I came here and after I came here. My mother, she was a musician of two notes.

Was it your mother that was, she isn't living now, is she? No, she passed. Didn't they call her Mother Richards? That's right. Because I went to the service once. Yes, you did. At the church way downtown. Yes, you did. You were playing. I know John and Ted Howard. Yes, I was. Yes, I was. We all, we all, we all. I remember your brother, your brother Julius the one that played guitar.
Was playing guitar.
Was playing guitar.
His name is Julius, right? That's right. He was there also. All of us was playing at the church at that time when she was speaking. And our, uh.
I wondered why her name was, they called her Mother Richards, I remember, wasn't it? That was her, that was her. Was it Richardson or Richards?
Richard. Mother Richards. Well that was her other marriage name.
I didn't know she just took that name as an evangelist. No, no. She was married. With the, for the Richardson.

She was married. She was married and, and, and her husband was a, was a, a preacher, was a spiritual preacher. Yes. And they, she carried his name after then. Yes. And that was the second time my mother had been married in her life. And my father, he had married about, he had married four times in life. Yes. But mother was married one time in life. Yes.
Now did she play any instruments or just sing? Piano.
Oh piano. Piano, yeah. She was a piano genius. She was a genius. She played in.
I guess I never heard her play.
No, I don't think so.
She played that night.

My mother played was in, in, in my hometown, past Christiane. Past Christiane. Uh-huh. But during that time she was a, before she was a pianist, she was an organist. They didn't have pianist during the time that she was.
Yes. I remember there was small organist. You'd pump up your feet.

That's right. That's right. She wasn't a pianist. Then the other boy, they didn't have pianist out. Yeah. And the first piano was in the church. Mm-hmm. On Davis Avenue. At Goodwill Baptist Church. She, uh, organized the piano there. It was so many knocks and so many pullbacks that they didn't want a piano. But still yet, through her, that they still put the piano in the church. Mm-hmm. And that was her, that was one of her chorales in life. That she had the first time to put a piano in the church. Yeah. Because all they had was an organ. Mm-hmm. And because they played the organ at, at fumes, or at a car. Yes, I know a lot of churches still use organ a lot too. Yeah. Yeah, that's right. But now they have pump organ, but during those times, they just had the pedal organ. Yeah. You understand? And she was the first one to have a piano in the church. And after then, well, they'd use the piano just for occasion of, uh, just in occasion of working. And a fume, they wouldn't have it. Yes. And they'd have it just in occasion of the choirs to sing. Mm-hmm. And they'd have it just for church.
Yes, I understand.

And afterward, if they had a fume, well, they'd, they'd, they'd, they'd play the piano for, for, for, for, for, for, for, for, for, for the fume request. You understand? But still yet, they had a lady by the name of Miss Fields. I can't recall her other name just now, but she was a Fields. And she'd taken with my mother and she was a pianist. And maybe years and years after then, she'd taken the piano over and she was teaching in the Sunday school and teaching. Still over in Pastor Christian. Still in Pastor Christian. And at Goodwill Baptist Church. All that was at Goodwill Baptist Church. Now, uh, after then, well, my brother, he came to the city of New Orleans. He stayed here for years.
And you came here in 1927. I wonder if there's anything else you could tell us about the music over in Pastor Christian, any of the, uh, bands. Were there any, uh, parade bands on the street?

Well, well, well, well, we had, we had, uh, one of the best, uh, parades. It was, I imagine, during the time that we had parades here, we had them in Pastor Christian. And we had some very, very wonderful flutes. Is that at Mardi Gras time? Mardi Gras times. Albert Alexander had flutes. He sat down and built flutes during the time that we have here today. And I guess that was in 1919 or 1902. We had regular carnival there just like we have here, floats and alls, and we had carnival there. And we was playing up and down the streets for the floats at that time. Well, my father and I and my brothers, my baby brother also, he was a guitar player from Boise. We was all musicians from Boise. Not at all. We had just a glorious time in Paschristian. Only time we had floats in. We never had any floats in Gulfport, Biloxel, Basel, Louis, just in Paschristian. Uh-huh. And we had glorious time there, just with floats. Well, after years that passed, well, this fella by name, my father bought all of us instruments, all kind of instruments, porcelain. Well, John, he learned clarinet and saxophone. Me, I learned bass violin. My baby brother, he learned guitar.
Were there any other brothers besides the two? No.
Just six of us in the family. Just six of us.
Girls play anything?
The girls? Yeah, my sister's a great pianist of today.
Oh, three boys, one girl, and your father and mother. That's right. That's right.

Six of us in the family. Six of us in the family. Well, we had two more, Eugene and another girl, but they passed as babies. They passed as babies. Twin to the guitar player. Oh, really? Yeah. He passed as a baby. Uh-huh. And my sister, other sister, she passed as a baby. Uh-huh. Now, Eugene was my twin brother's brother. And the other girl, she was, I just remember her name now, because she passed as a baby also. And therefore, well, it was just six of us right up and we are still all together, four of us is all together today. That's nice. Up until now. And you take Tom Albert. Do you know him?
Oh, yes. He used to play violin and then carnet, too. Right.

Right. Tom Albert. Taking my oldest brother. He was a planet wizard. Brought in here to the city of New Orleans from Paschkee Stanton. And they played and they played all in Lafayette. I think Tom Albert's from, he's from Lafayette or somewhere up the road.
Yeah, he came over on the other side of the river there.
Yeah, on the other side of the river, right. And he's taken my brother and he made histories of him through in his life.
Well, after then, I'd taken sick.

And I came here with pennies. I just remember the fellow I was working for, but he was from, he was from over the river. And he had a summer home in Long Beach. And I had a girlfriend. And I was with that girlfriend and through that girlfriend, I would go on her job. And I'd taken from there, the doctor taking in with me. I'd do a little days work, a little, in and out once in a while. And they'd taken a liking to me and I fell sick with a penny. Then I came here. They brought me here. They brought me on Tulane. And when they brought me on Tulane, my mother was living here, my mother and my sister, up in Carlton. Then they gave me a note. I wasn't living here. My mother and them was here already. But I wasn't living here. But they gave me a note to go to the Charlie Hospital. Old Charlie. That's where I was operating in. Old Charlie for pennies. I left from there. I went back by my mother and them up in Carlton Avenue. I was there about, about nine weeks. Then I had a job that offered to me. The sand caused down. And at that time, they had a thinner to take all the paint off the cars and make it just sit. Just bring it back to the natural tin. Then we'd take gasoline and wash it down good. Then sand it again. If you didn't sand it good, that the paint would raise and it wouldn't be a good job. So we had to wash it down. Then go over it with vinegar to make everything blend out so it would be a good job. Well during those times I met a lot of musicians such as our Kid Rainy. I met our Kid Punch. I met Buddy Petit.
I didn't meet the greatest man he is now.
Louis Armstrong.
Louis Armstrong. I didn't meet him during those times.
I guess he went to Chicago.
Yeah, he was in Chicago.

Before we go on with that part of your life, I was wondering if you could tell us more about how you took up the base, how old you were, and who helped you? Did your father help you? Or who did you teach you? Or what happened?
No teacher.
No teacher. Just picked it up.
My father had a band. Just like we would be here. And he would call a rehearsal. And they called a rehearsal. And the fellow was named Selby Thomas.
He had a fine bass.

I often tried to get that violin after he died and after I was grown. It was an old time old, big old violin. But that thing carried. It was the best violin that you wanted to see. It was large. It wasn't like mine, three quarters. It was an oversized, oversized. And it was really a fine violin. And in the beginning of my life, before I ever take up to try to learn violin, I'd take chair rounds. At that time, they had chair rounds. And chair. And I would take that chair round and I'd rub it on my finger. Oh yeah, I've seen people do that. And make bass out of that.
Mm, mm, mm, mm, mm, mm, mm, mm, mm, mm, mm, mm, mm, mm, mm, mm.
The harder you rub, the more different sound you would get out of it. How do you hold that finger on the... On the... On the...
Just like I'd hold it on a table or on a chair or anything.
And I'd get the sound of the bass on that... On this finger. I've heard that. I once heard Slowgag do that once. Well... He held his finger on the door.
I think.
Yeah, huh. Well, that's right.
Years ago, I saw him do that.
I could take this finger and take a chair round right now and kind of wet it a little bit. And rub it over that finger and make any kind of tune of V. Sounds good, yeah.
Yeah, sounds good.
Anytime... It's not loud enough to make anything out of it. In a big band.
That's right. You know what I mean?

But I could take that finger and make any kind of note I want with as invatizing of a bass. Well, I did that for years. And my father and them, they called a rehearsal. And as they would call a rehearsal, and when the bass player would get up to go to the bathroom or somewhere, well, I'd get up in that finger with his violin. And I'd begin to catch on more and more and more and more and more. Well, after then, well, I'd become to like it and still love it, and I don't think I'll ever hate it. No. Well, I have had all kinds of instruments. I've had trombone. I've had drums. I have cornet. I have tri... Uh, violin. My father bought everything that we thought that we might want to take up in instrument line. Well, I thought I would like drums very much. I kept on drums a long time. All right. After then, I pick up trombone. I was good on trombone.
You didn't really learn about that?

I really was good on trombone. Well, some reason, I don't know. I forgot about the trombone and got back on my violin. I guess that was my gift. And I stayed on violin up until the day. And right now, I don't think I could hit a lick on the drums anymore. And I don't have any more teeth. I know I can't play trombone anymore.
Every night...
Then after I was here, I tried to take a tuba. But I didn't have the bass tuba. I had the altor or whatever you would call it.
Maybe it's something called baritone.

That was the baritone tumor. I didn't have the bass. And I had a fella. He was very nice to me. He's dead now. And he lent me notes. And he showed me the notes of bass horn. And the cliffs of bass horn and the bass violin. And the same. No different whatsoever. It's nothing but some difference. It's in trombone. A little bit off the cliffs of bass violin. That was our...
He did. God bless him.
I think of his name before you leave. But right now, I can't. We work at Budweiser together. I played bass violin at Budweiser for years and years. And I can't think of his name. Booker. Booker.
Booker.
You remember Booker?
I don't remember. No.

You don't recall Booker? He was an old time musician. And he'd been in the local for years. He was working. No, he wasn't working at the time of Gagli killed the... That man killed Gagli. Walter Decker. Yeah, he wasn't working. He wasn't working there then. Mm-hmm. They had laid the bass off. Because this thing got bad and he wasn't working there. But he was the whole bass player there at the Budweiser at that time. But anyway...
Where did you get your first bass then? Uh...
A coincidence. When I was small, before I had a bass... I had one. No, thank you. No. And uh... My instrument was made out of a soap box.
Oh, Slowdrag made one of homemade ones too. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. And uh... We were um... Made it out of a soap box. And ironed into whether you believe it or not. Julius Handy, Sylvester Handy, and John Handy was playing mandolin. My oldest brother was playing mandolin. We was always musicians. He played mandolin, John Handy, Julius Handy on guitar, Sylvester Handy on bass. And my bass was made out of a soap box. So... It had a string, string tree out of it. Three strings, three strings. Yeah. You understand? Every second of it. And you wouldn't imagine during those times, people would all plop down south from Chicago, New York, and everywhere. And we made more money then and we make snow from music. That's about to get away. We did. We did. Was that in Paschristian? In Paschristian. In Paschristian. We had... We... It's still there, the Marymo Hotel. Every Wednesday, we had an engagement at the Marymo Hotel. And we'd go there and we'd play from 6 until 7 or 7.30 during meal time. While they was in there eating, we would be there playing soft, entertaining them while they was eating. And I'd have my soap box up in there. And they'd just... I'm telling you, I made more money off of that and I made off my real volume.
Yeah, but you did.

I did. In fact, all of us did good. We all did good. In the middle of the night. When someone else had joined us, which was called... Anyway, I can't think of his name just now. But he joined us, him and a lady. And that was the old cakewalk. Him and his wife did an old cakewalk. And something you don't see today anymore.
No.

But they did the old cakewalk and we made money together. All of us. That was five of us together. And we made money off of those two people and those two people made money off of us. Then, you say, on a Tuesday or other nights, we would visit other homes. We would call that a sunate. We would go to their home and ease up there and all of a sudden we just strike out with a tune, you know. And the people were just thrilled over that. And we made money.
We made money.

We don't make no money today. With all we do up in the Correa, with all we do in the Union and everything, we don't make the money that we made when I was a kid. We don't make that kind of money anymore.
Times have changed.

Yes. I tell you what, my mother, I'd go home with 30, 40 dollars and give my mother. And it would seem impossible for us to pick up that kind of money, a piece to go home with. And we have made good money. Made good money. Then I've had cousins and they would likewise. It wasn't three, it was six of us all together. My cousin and I and my brothers. And they'd go around, we called it Surinating and we'd go around Surinating. And we would make, we have made some money during those times. Well, after then, after I came to the city of New Orleans, I played with Kid Quencher, I played with Kid Rainey, I played with Louis Armstrong. During the time he come from Chicago here and he have had our, uh, come down here short of a bass player. Well, I sat in with them. Of course, now I didn't get any money. But I was too glad just to say that I played with the best of, the best of musicians. Then I have worked with our Sydney Dasgene for money.
We can turn this off for a minute.
I see she taking.
Hold on.
Just, just go ahead on, Doc. And I, I worked with Sydney Dasgene for years and years and years. Oh yeah. And I, uh.
I heard his big band several, many years ago.
Yeah. I worked, I worked with him, yeah. And he had a bass player.
Yeah, okay.
So when did you finally get your bass? Did you have a bass over in Pasch-Christian or wait until you got over here? Yeah, I know I had bass in Pasch-Christian. Man.

I had, I had several basses in Pasch-Christian. I had basses that they, they broke up for me and then I, I, I left a piece of bass in Pasch-Christian when I came here. Well, when I came here, I gave up music. I didn't intend to play anymore. Oh really? No, I didn't intend to play anymore. Well, after I got here and I began to go around and mix with different people, then they, we could, they got up a band by the name of the Rapsodians.
Rapsodians? I don't know.
No, I imagine you didn't. I don't think you were here.
No, I know I wasn't ever around in those days.

No. Well, we had, we have a 12 piece band and their name was the Rapsodians and they kept on after me, kept on after me to, they heard about me and kept on after me to, to play with them. I said, well, I don't have any violin while I left my violin in Pasch-Christian.
We can move this.

And I, I didn't care about playing anymore. Well, after I didn't care about playing anymore, they say, well, beans is there, I'll buy your violin. Well, I say, I don't have any money, which I didn't have. Then I was so independent then, I didn't think credit count was any way. And I was sticking on my chest. Who me? No, indeed. I don't want you to buy me no violin. I, what I get, I'll pay cash for it. Well, I was thinking that if you was a big shot, you pay for what you're getting. That was over with, but that wasn't anything. And I went to a wire line and they asked me about my credit card. I said, I don't have any. I thought I was smart. You understand? I said, what I get, I'll pay for it. I was sticking out my chest. I pay for what I get and I don't, I don't get nothing on credit. Smart, you understand? I thought I was smart, but I was dumb. And they told me, he said, now, Handy, I'm going to tell you, see, if you don't have a credit card you're not recognized. See, they have people really have nothing but some money and they have a credit account because they wanted their name to be enlisted in the book to be recognized as someone. Well, I still couldn't see it. You understand? Well, I still take me that, that granted that I had, I was something that could stick out my chest pocket here for everything I'll get.
How much did they want for a bass? I guess they're expensive. How much were the basses there?

Well, they had one for, they had several cheap basses. Well, a big three-quarter bass like I was telling you about the fella had over home. But I didn't like that. I was kind of concerned about a small bass. It's right there, right now. Right back here. Right back here. It's back there in the resort. And I hit on this, I hit on several other basses. They sounded all right. But when I hit on this one, it gave me the natural tone and I liked the way it sounded. So I said, how much is this violin? That violin there cost me $390-something.
I said, I like that very much.

All right. Beans, they say, you like that? I say, yes, sir. He said, well, he likes this violin. How much is this violin? They told him $300-something. He said, how much, Sylvester, how much you want to put out on it? I look at Beansie, you know, I ain't had nothing to put out on it. You understand? So, he looked back at me and I looked back at him and he said, well, I put $100 down on it. And they made arrangements for Beansie to take out so much every month or every week.
Yeah.

On the violin while I was working for them. I was working for him every Sunday night. Sometime through the week, because I know how many bands would come in town. And sometime I'd sit in there, Louis Armstrong would come in town. I'd sit in and work with him. Well, they didn't give me anything, but I imagined that they would give him all. Well, I said what it was. It didn't make anything to me. I was too glad to say that I was working with Louis Armstrong to receive anything. You understand? Yeah. And I still was with the Rhapsody and we worked from the Estores over to our... Over to our...
Did you have the San Jacinto then?

The San Jacinto. We worked from Rhapsody to San Jacinto. And we had nice engagements from jobs to jobs, you know. And there for a while. Beansie still would take out the money for his violin until it was paid for. Well, after it was paid for, they had another fella by the name of Jerry Green. And Jerry Green, he joined the band, which was a bass player, and he'd taken the violin over. And he worked with them for years and years and years. After then, the band broke up for some cause. And then the violin come back to me and I have the violin yet. But Jerry, he was working with the band. And on a picnic, some woman fell in the violin and broke it in. And after then, well, I take the violin back over and I was working with the different band. And I worked with Papa Celestan. I worked with Kid Randy. I worked with Kildee.
You heard it back? No, you can hear it. I don't know. I've heard of it. You heard of it.
You don't know?
No, I don't remember. I've only been around here. I started coming around here in 1937, but I didn't move here until about six and a half years ago. I see. I see.

He died, but I still work with so many different other fella. Now they have a little fella. And then I work with Andrew Morgan's brother. Sam Morgan. Sam Morgan. Sam Morgan. I work with Sam. I work with Isaiah. I work with Sam. And I work with the saxophone player. And then I work with him. And they have another little kid that is real famous, which would be our... Sam Morgan. He's a... He's a... His brother's a great drummer. And he amitated Lewis Armstrong so much.
I have a... Speaking of recording, did you ever make any records?
Well, I made records with you.
Yes, I mean, were there any records in the old days, though?
Uh, honey. Hmm? Who was that I made records with and it never went over? Can you recall?
No, you was with John Hadney and...
No, darling, before then. We made... They didn't have... They had a recording machine on Ramport Street there some way.
Oh, I forgot that.
And we made some records and they never went over.
They never did come out?
No. They never issued? No, they never issued them. But I can't recall what band I was with then.
I can't even...
But Smiley Louis, Smiley George...
I think...

I can't just recall. But anyway, I played with Gilbert. Gilbert Young. You know Gilbert Young? I played with Gilbert Young. I imagine... I couldn't tell you exactly how many I have right off the reel, you know? But after you leave, I imagine it's different people I could recall that I can't just now. But anyway, I...
I was wondering, it seems like somebody told me maybe your brother or somebody thought you'd made some records with Joe Robichaux. Do you remember? I did.

I did. That's right. That's what I say. After you would... After you leave, I could recall and I have made a record with Joe Robichaux. And Joe Robichaux and I, we've been all in Texas, County, Texas. And we had some nice engagements up there.
Where did you make the records with Joe Robichaux?
And, uh, wait now, they had a recording place on our...
Ramport?
Well, it was on Ramport or on Tulad.
I just...
Where was that big recording place there in town? The only recording place was...
There used to be one for a while in the late years on about Dumain and...
North Ramport. That's right. That's where we was. J and M, I think they called it. On Dumain and North Ramport. Then we had another...
Years ago, they made them down at the Godshaw Building, different places on Canal Street, I think, somewhere.
Well, we had a WWL or something like that.
Oh, yeah, that's right. They made them sometime at the radio station, too.

That's right. That's where we made them at the radio station. WWL at the radio station. We recorded that with the Rhapsodians. Then I recorded some on Dumain Street with Joe Robichaud. But either one of them come out. Either one of them come out. Of course, I'm not sure.
Well, the problem I think of, but who else was in the Rhapsodians of that band? Can you remember who else played any of the trumpets and trombones and all of the other...

Many of the members? Uh, Kerry Levine was a saxophone player. He was a sweet saxophone player. Very young. He was about 19 or 20. He was very young. And, uh... We had another one about the name of... I can't recall his name now, but he was a sweet alto also. And... Little Johnny, or Johnny or Little John, he lives uptown now. He's always on the road. He was a sweet trumpet player. Very young stuff. Very young stuff. He was a sweet trumpet player, and still is a sweet trumpet player. His name was John, John something. Pardon me. Pardon. And, uh... This same fella, Frog, we called him Frog. Oh yeah.
Waldron Joseph. Yeah.

We called him Frog. He's a cripple. On trombone. He was a sweet... He's still a sweet guy. Yeah, he's still playing nice. He's still a sweet guy. Well, we called him Frog. And, uh... It's a trumpet player by the name of Lucky.
You wouldn't even know him, I don't think. Just not.

He had a long, steeple head. But he was above Louis Armstrong, hitting high notes. He'd go just like if you take your mouthpiece out of your trumpet and just blow your mouthpiece and hit a note. But he'd hit that note with that mouthpiece and that trumpet. He'd go higher than Louis Armstrong. What's his name again?
Uh...

We called him Lucky, but his right name... I couldn't call his right name right now, but we called him Lucky. But he could hit any kind of note on that trumpet. He was really good. He was really good. And they had my boy Frog, he was on trombone. And he still is on trombone.
Did he have a piano player in the band?

Yes, we did. And the piano player, I can't call his name now. Uh... Uh... He's a... I think his name was Earl... Earl something. But anyway, he's still playing and he have a... A piano that takes around by hand now. It's a small... Yeah, a small piano. He takes around by hand. But I can't call his name. Remember the drummer in the band?
Did you tell me the drummer? Yeah. Um...

I couldn't recall his name right now. And at the time we had a little fellow on the guitars. I think you remind me. By the name of Jimmy. He had one of the... One of the outstanding guitars. Because he had a steel guitar. Steel. It wasn't like these today. Like the Hawaiian? No, it was something like a banjo. Oh, I see. It was a round... A round steel guitar. Made on steel, yeah. A round steel guitar. I don't see any... Since you recall in my mind, I haven't saw it for years. I don't even see it in the showcases anymore. But it was made something under the honor of a banjo. But it had the curves in it, just like my bass violin. But still, it was a steel one. It was a steel guitar. And he played that steel guitar for years and years with us. And I haven't saw that in years to pass. His name was Jimmy. Now...
Any of your brothers play in the band? No, no.
Not with me during those times. During those times. And I played with little local bands, such as The Chic and... And this fellow with blue so large, Sam... Sam who? Sam...
I can't think.
On trumpet? Yeah.
I can't even think. Oh, anyway, it's Sam. I'll think of it.
He waits for the...
For the hog, for the... What's our insurance, baby? Oh, it was a Joseph Raymond. What's his name?
What's our insurance? Sweetheart. Our insurance was... The Acme insurance was... Sam... They call him Sambo sometimes? Sambo. Sambo. Joseph is his last name.
What's his first name? I don't know.
I can't think. I don't know. Anybody need to live? I'll work with him. Then I'll work with Sheik. I'll work with so many... I work with so many.
I know how it is here. They work with everybody.

Yeah, I can't just recall all of them. Even down to Kildee, you know Kildee? You mentioned that. Yeah, when I work with our... They have a fellow, a little youngster. He was pretty good. He went into TB and he came. I think he's in Biloxi in the hospital or something. Nah, I can't recall his name.

Well, I think I was going to ask about the left-handed bass. You're a left-handed bass player. I noticed Mr. Kimball, Narvin Kimball, some people call him Henry Kimball, Jr., plays left-handed too. I wonder, did you ever change... Is your bass changed over? Did you change the sound post or anything? Or how do you do that?
Just like it is.
The same as any other bass you play? Right, right.
Nothing changed. Just like a right-hand man, I can get up. Now, Kimball bass, I can't play yet. It's strung up left-handed.
Yes, I know, yes.

It's Richard Voic, it's for him. Well, if any way he working, I can't work his instrument. Any right-hand man, I can work the instrument. Because Selby Thomas was a right-hand man. Then I used to get up and... Play a little...
Play a little...
And that's the way I learned off of his violin. And as I learned off of his violin, I can't play in the other way, but the way it's strung up right-handed. That's the only way I can play.
You played left-handed, though, in those days, too,

and you started... I still, yeah. That's just the way I taught. That's the way I am today. I've never changed. I've never... I've tried Kimball's violin, but I couldn't make any headway with it because it's strung up times. I couldn't even make a C chord on his instrument because it's awkward to me. It's like a left-hand man would grab my violin and couldn't play my violin. I grab his violin, I can't play his violin because mine's strung up for right-handed. And it's just...
When you started out, did you pick or bow mostly?
Well, both of them. Both of them. I bowed. And I liked the bowing. I liked the bowing very much.
They don't use much bowing nowadays.

No, they don't bow very little. You catch the best of the violin playing, the biggest instrument, biggest band in here. They have bowing where they have a whole lot of cellars. They have bowing with beats, but outside of that, you don't catch that anymore. It's all picking. All picking. So, there for a while. I just got away from bowing. Just got away from bowing, but I used to bow good. I used to bow good. I used to love it, too. Used to love it.
Oh, yeah.

Used to love it. But after style commenced getting greater and greater and greater and greater and greater, and I just began to just go head on, and I just pick instead of bowing. And I feel that, I tell you one thing, though, honestly, here's some slow numbers. Here's some slow numbers. If you were bowing, it would sound greater, greater than picking. Yeah, because the tone is the same. Yeah, it would pull the whole value of the tone out if you were bowing. Because if you pull that bow and hold that bow, the slowness would still carry the melody and the tone of bowing more than if you hit it that lick.
Yeah, I think so.

Then you're not supposed to hit it two, two-fold, or three-fold. You're supposed to hit boom. Well, if you're pulling that boom, it would be... Yeah, you keep on holding it all out. Yeah, holding that note out, which you have in your music, a whole note, a half note, a whole sound, and so on. Well, that's in music, but still, if you're picking it, you can't get that whole note out of that because the tone would leave. And I believe if you were bowing it, you could make a whole note carry just like it's supposed to be on music.
Yeah, they could sell it.
You understand? But still, yeah. It's a vast, even on TV. I don't see them bowing no more. No, I never.
Not very, very seldom.

If they're in a large, large 12- or 15-piece orchestra, well, with sort of the cellos and the orchestra, then all of them bow. The beast bowing the cello bow also. But just a beast sticking out, it's nothing but stick out today. You just have to stick out. That's all. And therefore, well, I've experienced a lot of it in life. And I'm just crazy if I'm a violin. That's all. It's not the one thing holds me up with my violin.
What's that?

That's when I want to stop and get a sandwich or something to bring home that I have to lock the car up and I still go backwards and find to see if someone's trying to break in the car to take it out. You understand? It's an awkward thing to carry. It is. You take like that and drums, they're awkward. They're awkward. You understand? And it just keeps you with a worried mind all the time. In the old days,
did you carry them on a streetcar?
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Yeah, we carried them lots on the streetcar. You can't get them on the bus now anymore. No, no. Well, I imagine you still could take them on a streetcar.
I suppose.

But I don't know. During once, you could take them and then you'd have to go to City Hall and get a pass to take them. Well, I heard that you had to get permits. That's right. To take them and then, well, it got so skeezy until I don't think to even worry about them anymore because I don't think... I never see anybody else. No one, everybody have automobiles to carry them. You understand? But during those times, you'd have to have a pass to take them on the streetcars. That was very inconvenient. That was very inconvenient. A bass violin is unconvinient, more unconvinient than a drum because you can just put a drum down anyway and it's not seen. But a bass violin, you got to throw it across the back of the car and it's very, very noticeable.
That's right.

Very more noticeable. So, therefore, it's more tempted to the public than any other instrument you have. And I'd like to have something that I have or never had. I imagine I would if I hear enough of it as a folding bass.
Oh, I've heard of them but I've never seen one.
I'd like to have it if it would give satisfaction. You understand?
I doubt it would be too good.

I don't think so. I don't see how it could be. I don't think so. I don't think so. But it would suit me for the getting out the way. Yeah, yeah. Getting out the way. You understand? It's just like that. Yeah, don't blame me for that. It's just like that folding piano. It's just like that. Well, you take a fellow, he have a folding piano. Well, he can pack it in and every way he go. But my violin, I can't succeed with it as much as a person can just pull up something and go along with it. So, and another thing, I don't know. I dislike the bass guitars.
Oh, those are the...
Imitating the bass. Yeah, I don't like that. They don't take the place of a violin. No, they don't take the place of a violin. Not to me.
Not to me.

They don't. But still yet, lots of people goes for that. Now, Mr. Bill, I'm going to tell you something. Friday night coming, it's going to have a van right around the corner if you can come out with it.
I'm going to be, I have to leave, I'm going to leave tomorrow night, I think. And go up to see my mother that, don't you?
Yeah, yeah, you did tell me. Well, anyway...
St. Louis or so by that time, I mean. Uh-huh.

Well, anyway, I want you to hear... I wish I could. I want you to hear this piano. Right around here, huh? Uh-huh. The next block. I'm going to inform you. Maybe later on, when I get back. They're supposed to be not signing a contract for so long over here at this boy room.
What street is it on?
That's on our room.
Gentilly down in there?
No, no. Not that far. The next corner from me. What's the next street, my lover? What? Next street, where, where, where, where, where, uh, where in that is? Uh, uh, something. Sumter Street.
Oh, yeah. That's one,
that's the next block.
Right over there? Yeah, right, even with me. Uh-huh. Even with me right here. There's another head of bar room over there.
Yeah, and, uh, they having a band over there, uh, on Fridays.
Yeah, be nice.

And I want you to, uh, hear them. They're youngsters. They're just coming out. They're youngsters. And, uh, the first time I heard them, they was real nice. Now, I don't know what they're going to produce from now on. Yeah, you never know.
They're still going to be good.
Well, they don't come on until nine. They play three hours from nine to twelve. Uh-huh. So, when, when they were...

I was going to ask you about some of the different places around the different neighborhoods you used to play. Did you used to play up at the Flunkin' Manny's, up at Shoppe Toulouse Street, way uptown there?
Where the road come into a point?
I don't remember exactly what street that was on. I never heard Kid Howard with the band

there once. Mr. Bill, I'm going to tell you I played so many places until I can't. In other words, I'm going to be frank with you. I don't know the city that well. But I can recall the playing everywhere in the city of New York.
All sorts of little halls and... That's right.

All over, I can recall the playing with some of everybody have had been in the city of New Orleans. And that's been all over. In town. Out of town. Now, I work with a... Fella from out of Manderville. He was over here at the club the other night. Oh, he's from Mandeville, a couple of them. They got a drummer from Mandeville. I just can't recall how many humans I have worked with.
I hear quite a few fellas say they came from across the lake there, too.
That's right, from Mandeville, and I work with them often and times after time, but I can't remember. I work with Earl Foster. I work with Earl Foster years and years.
Yes, Andy Anderson was raised over there, too.
Who?
Andy Anderson, the trumpet player, I think.
Is it Andrew? Andy Anderson.
He plays with John Kazimer.
Yeah, he's Anderson. Yeah, he was up at the hall the other night when I came to talk to you. He was up at the hall the other night. Yeah, I work with him. I was like, yes.

Well, there's one question while I think I was going to ask. It might be your brother. Somebody seems to... told me about that somebody had some cylinder, made some cylinder records. You remember those little tiny round records that go around about the size of a glass and they go on a machine? Somebody made some of those here a long time ago. Somebody said when you all were kids they had them. Somebody had the name of Tunstall or something, a name like that. Tunstall. Tunstall, I don't know how you pronounce it. Made some band, made some of those cylinders. If you don't remember, some of those were made, they called an Edison machine. Edison phonographs. It used cylinders, basically having a flat disc type. Yeah, I understand. It was on the type of this mic. Yeah, on the type of this mic.

Yeah, on the type of this mic. Round cylinder. I can't recall that, but I can't recall who it was with now. But I can picture what you're speaking about. It was just about the size of this glass. And it was just like if you was playing in one of those old time photographs.
Oh, that's the old time.
Yeah, one of those old time photographs like you was playing in. But, let me get my thoughts together. It's been a long time.
Yes, it was hard to remember way back.
Yeah, it seems if it was in a speaker that didn't have any electric. No, they didn't have electric. It was a speaker that people would speak through. Yeah, they do things like that.
Yeah, they record into it too.

That's right. That's right. But I just can't get it straight right now. I just can't recall. You called my remembrance back to something that have been years ago that I can't just relate right now. I just can't relate. I understand you. It's hard to remember. It's hard for me to get back to that part of it. But, uh...

Well, I was going to ask some more about the old times. In the back and past Christiana, the bands, what did they sound like? Say that trio, what kind of music did you play for the serenades? Was it like dance music or more like popular songs or waltzes or what kind of music did they play? What pieces remembered?

Probably you would understand and probably you wouldn't and probably it would be just in my way of speaking. Or maybe it would be out of my way of speaking, but I'm going to see it this way. Which they would ask us before we'd come in to play dinner dance, dinner songs. Which is Old Black Joe and I'm Coming and maybe a cakewalk dance or some sentimental numbers. Something sweet that they would, but we'd ease in the dining, next to the dining would be playing sweet numbers while they was eating nothing jassy or nothing that would excite them or anything. Just something to amuse them that they was eating and it would be pleasing to the ear that they was having a nice, quiet supper. That's the type of music we'd be waking on. But now if we'd walk up to someone's door and they would be eating or something would be happening that they would be all quiet inside. We'd play the numbers that Old Black Joe and we'd play the numbers that would be some kind of a jazz of our type during those times, which I can't recall. Yes, I know you got it. Because they were too old for me to recall them back today.
What was the dance music like though then when you'd play for a dance or something? Was it as fast as it is now or?
Oh yes.
What kind of a?
Pardon me. Oh yes. We'd play jazz. We'd play like we'd play for dance halls or for dances or anywhere we'd be called on. Well that was a larger band than three pieces.
Oh yes, it would be bigger.

It would be six or seven pieces that were during my father's time and I was playing with my father or something like that. And my father would play real music or maybe you would call a hillbilly today because lots of them would get out there and do the card trill. Well that's the type of thing. Yeah, and they would do our, let me see. And they'd do a whole lot of clapping and keeping time with the music. Well I would say a card trill. I would say they would do a card trill dance during those times.
You understand what I'm speaking about? Yes, I've seen some of that.
And we'd play modeling music during those times while they had what you call the shimmy she wobble. Oh yeah.
I remember what that was. I remember.

And they'd have the throwing out the halls and this one would dance with that one and then line this one would dance with that one. Because if they shake up to their lady they'd throw them out and cause a big fight and so on.
You understand?

But they wouldn't realize that what would come up to the day. Now you shake with anybody's wife and if you don't shake you're not dancing. But during them times they'd call that a ratty dance. You understand? They didn't like nobody to shake with their wife. And during the times, during them times I was playing with my father and as I was playing with him while we'd play all types of music. We'd play jazz while we learned jazz from children. It's been jazz ever since I've been a baby. Up until now. We'd play a sweet and a little music. We'd play seminal music. Then we'd play jazz. Just the same as it is today. Only I imagine, I don't see much difference in it today than it was in my time of coming, unless you just wanted to make a little addition. Because we were all brought up on jazz as long as I know the world we've been brought up on jazz music. Jazz music is not brought from the city of New Orleans. Jazz music is brought from the countries.
You think it started in the countries?
In the countries. That's where jazz music started. Every jazz band you know of is not originated from the city of New Orleans. It's originated from the country.
A lot of the fellows did come from outside of the city.

All of them came from outside of the city. None of them born and raised here would bring up jazz. The ones with no jazz come from the ones that came from out of the country and brought it into the city of New Orleans or any other state. It's no one have really ran up into a big town that knew jazz before some country person brought it to that town. Jazz is brought from some region nation just from mother wit. It's not from writing of music. It's brought from mother wit, from somebody from some far country. Wherever it is in the big cities, it wasn't ran up there. Just like you would take old region nine quartet of spiritists. It's brought from the countries.
You think the music of the church had much to do with influencing the dance music and jazz? That's right. That's right.
They have a lot of it. It's the biggest jazz it is now. It's the pianist of the church. Brings the jazz of the spiritual of the harmonized in the churches from the country.
They have that same kind of a beat in it.
That's right. That's right. And right now you take the biggest church it is, the pianist of, have as much jazz in it today that the bands of musical have.
There was a good pianist over there with the two singers, gospel singer Sunday over there across the street from me. Jazz.

It's a wonderful pianist. Jazz. Jazz. Jazz. Jazz. Jazz. Jazz. Jazz. Jazz. a city feeling because the city feelings would forbid that until they did do it at my home also. My mother had all touches of jazz and she had the touches of blues. I didn't know anything about it during those times. But still yet, as time growed, I could find the feelings and know the feelings of it. And the choir would sing much more.
